hints: Start with Fig. 5.1. The cat shows the recessive phenotype for both traits, so think about what that tells you about the alleles it must carry.
The other parent is described as heterozygous for both genes, so think about how many different allele combinations independent assortment can make in its gametes.
Remember the two genes are unlinked, so H/h and R/r assort independently when you list gametes.
Pair the single gamete type from the recessive parent with each of the four gamete types from the heterozygous parent to get the F1 genotypes.
For each F1 genotype, check if a dominant H or R is present to decide short vs long hair and full colour vs pointed.
walkthrough:
Work Out The Two Parent Genotypes**
A recessive phenotype can only appear when no dominant allele is present. The Fig. 5.1 cat is long hair (hh) and pointed (rr), so it must be $hhrr$. The other cat is heterozygous for both genes, so it must be $HhRr$. Its phenotype must show both dominants: short hair full colour.

List Gametes Using Independent Assortment**
The $hhrr$ parent can only make $hr$ gametes. Because the genes are unlinked, the $HhRr$ parent makes four gamete types in equal numbers: $HR$, $Hr$, $hR$, $hr$. This is the classic test-cross pattern.

Combine To Get F1**
Join $hr$ with each of the four types: $hr + HR = HhRr$, $hr + Hr = Hhrr$, $hr + hR = hhRr$, $hr + hr = hhrr$. Then translate: any $H-$ is short hair, $hh$ is long hair, any $R-$ is full colour, $rr$ is pointed. That gives all four phenotype combinations in 1:1:1:1.

Final answer: parent phenotypes: long hair pointed x short hair full colour; parent genotypes: $hhrr \times HhRr$; gametes: $hr$ from $hhrr$ and $HR$, $Hr$, $hR$, $hr$ from $HhRr$; F1 genotypes: $HhRr$, $Hhrr$, $hhRr$, $hhrr$ in equal 1:1:1:1 ratio; F1 phenotypes: short hair full colour, short hair pointed, long hair full colour, long hair pointed in equal ratio.

hints: Look in Fig. 5.2 for a pair of full colour (black symbols) parents that have a pointed (white symbol) son - think about what that means for alleles they must both carry.
walkthrough:
Spot The Hidden Allele Pattern**
If pointed were dominant, two pointed parents could have full colour children, but two full colour parents could never have a pointed child unless they were both carrying a hidden allele. In Fig. 5.2 the full colour female $-/+$ $4/6$ crossed with the full colour male $-/+$ $4/7$ have a pointed son $-/-$ $3/4$. That son shows $-/-$, no restriction site, which matches the r allele description. The only way this happens is if pointed is $rr$ recessive and both full colour parents are $Rr$ carriers.
Final answer: Two full colour cats produce a pointed offspring, e.g. the middle $ -/+ \times -/+$ cross produces a $-/-$ pointed son, so pointed must be recessive.

hints: Focus on the males in Fig. 5.2 and count how many marker alleles and how many +/- symbols each male has.
Think about what you would expect if the gene was on the X chromosome - how many alleles would a male have and from which parent would a son get his X?
walkthrough:
Why Males Rule Out X-Linkage**
A male mammal is XY, so for an X-linked gene he would have only one allele. Here every male in Fig. 5.2 has two marker numbers, e.g. $2/4$, $1/2$, $4/7$, and two +/- symbols, e.g. $-/-$ or $-/+$. That is only possible on an autosome where both homologues are present.

Check Father-To-Son Transmission**
With X-linkage a son gets his X only from his mother, never from his father. Here sons clearly get one marker number from the father, for example the top left $-/-$ $2/4$ father passes 2 or 4 to his daughter and son. Coat colour of sons is also not determined by the mother alone. So the R/r gene cannot be X-linked, it must be autosomal.
Final answer: Autosomal because males show two alleles for the marker and for +/- , e.g. $ -/+$ $4/7$; sons receive a marker allele from their father, so inheritance is not X-linked only from mother.

hints: Track each +/- symbol together with the marker number below it through parents to offspring - do they stay together as a block?
Look at the bottom right pointed son $ -/-$ $3/4$ and ask where his 3 and 4 came from and whether any new +/- with marker combinations appear.
walkthrough:
See The Block Inheritance**
Pick a chromosome, for example the full colour father $+/+$ $6/7$ passes $+6$ to his daughter and $+7$ to his son. The mother passes $-4$ with $-4$. The +/- state and the marker number travel together every time. That co-segregation means the marker locus is on the same chromosome very close to R/r.

No Crossing Over Products**
If the loci were far apart, crossing over would shuffle them and make new combinations like a $+$ with 3 or 4, or a $-$ with 7 in the grandchildren. The bottom right son is $-/-$ $3/4$, getting $-3$ from his mother and $-4$ from his father, exactly the parental blocks with no shuffling. No recombinants are observed, supporting close linkage.

Final answer: +/- and marker allele are inherited together as a block, e.g. $-4$ with $-4$, $+6$ with $+6$; no recombinants such as $+3$, $+4$ or $-7$ are seen in offspring, so loci are closely linked.
